image.subject: A split composition: on the left, a rumpled grey field uniform draped over the back of a chair beside a radio tracking console in a dark vehicle, headphones resting on the seat; on the right, a faded blue cotton dress hanging on a wooden peg in a cramped attic beside a small round window with pale Atlantic light streaming in

left.label: WERNER — LOOKED AWAY
left.subject: An 18-year-old German soldier with striking white-blond hair, pale skin, sharp intelligent blue eyes, lean wiry build, wearing a rumpled grey Wehrmacht field uniform with radio headphones around his neck, sitting at a radio tracking console in a dark military vehicle, his hand on the dial, eyes cast downward in shame

right.label: MARIE-LAURE — SAW CLEARLY
right.subject: A slight 16-year-old French girl with cloudy pale eyes from congenital cataracts, wavy dark brown hair pulled back with a ribbon, delicate cheekbones, wearing a faded blue cotton dress with a small leather satchel, standing in a cramped attic with her hands outstretched, face tilted upward with calm certainty

storyboard.claim: Werner chose to tune out atrocities; Marie-Laure, living in physical darkness, saw the world with perfect moral clarity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split-screen comparison: Werner hunched over his tracking equipment avoiding reality vs. Marie-Laure standing in Etienne's attic with open, fearless composure despite her blindness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Personalizes the previous beat's thesis about millions choosing moral blindness — these two characters embody opposite responses.
storyboard.addedInformation: The contrast: the sighted soldier who chose blindness vs. the blind girl who chose to see.

image.subject: A slight 16-year-old French girl with cloudy pale eyes from congenital cataracts, wavy dark brown hair pulled back with a ribbon, delicate cheekbones, wearing a faded blue cotton dress with a small leather satchel, fingertips tracing the air in front of her, standing on the rocky Atlantic shore below Saint-Malo's walls, grey waves crashing behind her, salt mist swirling around her, face radiant with understanding as pale light breaks through storm clouds above

storyboard.claim: Because Marie-Laure rigorously attended to the truth of her environment, her physical blindness became perfect moral sight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Marie-Laure on the shore below Saint-Malo, storm light breaking through clouds behind her — physical darkness around her, clarity in her expression.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the compare by landing on Marie-Laure's side — she is the proof that true sight is moral, not optical.
storyboard.addedInformation: Doerr's thesis crystallized: rigorous attention to truth is the real faculty of sight.

image.subject: A vintage radio transmitter with glowing amber vacuum tubes sitting on a worn wooden table, copper coils wrapped around a cylindrical core, a single beam of warm light illuminating the device in an otherwise dark room, loose handwritten pages scattered around its base

storyboard.claim: The ultimate weapon is not the bomb but the frequency we tune to, the stories we believe, and whether we hoard or broadcast knowledge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three-item list building on screen — each line landing like a verdict, no image needed because the rhetorical force carries it.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE FREQUENCY WE LISTEN TO / THE STORIES WE BELIEVE / THE KNOWLEDGE WE SHARE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from Marie-Laure's personal clarity to the universal principle — what are the real weapons in the war for perception.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the entire war narrative: the incendiary bomb is secondary to the contest over information and belief.

image.subject: A glowing radio transmitter with coiled copper wires and a warm amber vacuum tube, sitting on a worn wooden table in a cramped dusty attic with wooden rafters, a single beam of light falling across it from a small round window, the transmitter casting long shadows — no people visible, just the machine and the light

storyboard.claim: The transmission of knowledge is the eternal battlefield — our perception of it dictates our morality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Etienne's radio transmitter in the attic, isolated in a shaft of light — the object that represents the entire war between broadcasting truth and suppressing it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Distills the three-item list into one thesis statement — knowledge transmission is the war that never ends.
storyboard.addedInformation: The radio is no longer a plot device; it is the book's central metaphor made physical.

image.subject: A modern analyst in a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, gesturing directly toward the viewer with one hand raised, standing in a softly lit studio space, expression serious and intent, as if delivering a final challenge

storyboard.claim: Doerr extrapolates this idea to the modern day — the narrator invites the listener to look around their own space.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The narrator as cutout, breaking the fourth wall, gesturing toward the viewer — the shift from historical analysis to direct address.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the 1944 thesis to the present — the narrator steps out of the book and into the viewer's room.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the bridge beat: the novel's ending mapped onto the listener's life right now.

image.subject: A faceless modern figure in a plain dark hoodie, illuminated by the blue glow of a screen, headphones on, sitting alone in a dim room, surrounded by faintly glowing concentric rings of light radiating outward through the air around them — visualizing the invisible electromagnetic waves filling the space

storyboard.claim: Look around your physical space right now — you are swimming in an ocean of invisible waves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Everyman figure sitting in a modern room, glowing rings of invisible signal radiating through the space — a visual echo of Etienne's attic transmitter, now surrounding the viewer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The narrator's direct address lands here — the Everyman figure is the viewer's stand-in, making the 1944 metaphor viscerally present.
storyboard.addedInformation: The room is full of signals the viewer cannot see, just as occupied France was full of broadcasts.

image.subject: An evening city skyline seen from a rooftop, warm lights glowing in apartment windows, faint aurora-like streaks of light in the sky above the buildings, a rooftop antenna silhouetted against the twilight sky

storyboard.claim: Wi-Fi, cell towers, targeted advertising algorithms, millions of texts and data points fly invisibly through the air around your head.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A four-item list stacking on screen — each modern frequency named, building the overwhelming inventory of invisible signals surrounding the viewer right now.
storyboard.onScreenText: WI-FI NETWORKS / CELL TOWERS / TARGETED ALGORITHMS / MILLIONS OF DATA POINTS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Itemizes the ocean of invisible waves from the previous beat — makes the abstract concrete with specific modern technologies.
storyboard.addedInformation: These are the modern equivalents of the Nazi propaganda broadcasts and Etienne's Resistance transmissions.

image.subject: A faceless modern figure in a plain dark hoodie standing at a crossroads in a grey city, one hand holding a glowing smartphone, the other hand reaching up toward a vintage radio antenna mounted on a rooftop above, faint concentric signal waves visible radiating from both the phone and the antenna

storyboard.claim: Are you passively letting these frequencies wash over you? Walking on autopilot? Who is controlling the transmitter in your life?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A crowd of Everyman figures walking on autopilot down a modern street, all absorbed in screens — the modern equivalent of the sighted citizens of Paris who chose not to see.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the inventory of signals into a direct challenge — the viewer is asked whether they are Werner (tuning out) or Marie-Laure (attending).
storyboard.addedInformation: The 'sighted people in Paris' callback — millions with working eyes choosing blindness, now reframed as screen-addicted moderns.

image.subject: A bright open doorway at the end of a dark corridor, warm golden sunlight streaming through, dust motes floating in the light, a single empty chair turned toward the doorway as if someone just stood up and walked into the light

storyboard.claim: When the system demands your silence, will you have the courage to open your eyes before they close?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The Everyman figure removing headphones and looking up into light — choosing to see, choosing courage over comfortable blindness. The final image of the entire video.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The closing challenge — after the question of beat 247, this is the call to action. The Everyman chooses sight.
storyboard.addedInformation: Echoes Frederick's refusal and Marie-Laure's clarity — the viewer is now the one who must choose.
